A:
Gap-and-craps.

Stocks keep opening with an upside gap, then going nowhere or fading the rest of the day.

This isn't new.

It's worse in small caps.

Since the inception of $IWM:

Holding only overnight: +703%
Holding only intraday: -54%
B:
Buying dips hasn't worked this year.

Neither has buying rallies.

In 2022, the S&P 500's average next-day return after a down day is -0.18%. After an up day, -0.16%.

This is only the 2nd year in history where both lost on average.

The other was 1932.
C:
Somebody's in trouble.

S&P 500 futures down 3%.

10-year Treasury futures down 1%.

In the past 25 years, there have been 2 days like that:

October 9, 2008
March 18, 2020

Looks like forced liquidation.
D:
Analysts are bailing.

Per Bloomberg, today they raised price targets on 62 S&P 500 stocks.

They cut targets on 162.

Net upgrades minus downgrades ranks in the bottom 1.5% of all days in over a decade.
E:
Retail traders are not feeling it.

Last week, they bought $19.9 billion of puts to open.

And $6.5 billion of calls to open.

That's the first time in history puts were 3x calls.

Welp.
F:
Dumb Money Confidence just jumped to the 3rd-highest reading in 25 years.

In 2021, high readings weren't a problem.

Otherwise, very high readings tended to precede modest gains at best, until sentiment reset.

Not perfect, tho.
G:
Broad participation.

All but 2 S&P 500 sectors recently had about 90% of their stocks above their 50-day moving averages.

Since 1957, the equal-weight S&P 500 showed gains over the next 6 months almost every time.

The only real failure was 1973.
H:
Breadth thrust.

The S&P 500 just had 5 straight days with more than 68% of its stocks advancing.

That ties the record, in data going back to 1928.
I:
Credit is cracking before stocks.

Over the past 20 years, credit spreads widened sharply while the S&P 500 wasn't even in a pullback yet 3 times.

All 3 led to bear markets.*

* Yeah yeah, tiny sample size.

h/t @sentimentrader
